claim: Human medial parietal cortex (MPC) is implicated in multiple cognitive processes including memory recall, visual scene processing and navigation.
source: Human medial parietal cortex (MPC) is implicated in multiple cognitive processes including memory recall, visual scene processing and navigation, and is a core component of the default mode network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations throughout the introduction section.

claim: Human medial parietal cortex is a core component of the default mode network.
source: Human medial parietal cortex (MPC) is implicated in multiple cognitive processes including memory recall, visual scene processing and navigation, and is a core component of the default mode network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and referenced with citation to Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010 in the introduction.

claim: Distinct regions of MPC exhibited differential functional connectivity with medial and lateral regions of ventral temporal cortex (VTC).
source: First, distinct regions of MPC exhibited differential functional connectivity with medial and lateral regions of ventral temporal cortex (VTC).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through resting-state functional connectivity analysis in Experiment 1.

claim: Medial regions of MPC showed selective, but negative, responses to the visual presentation of different stimulus categories, with clear preferences for scenes and faces.
source: Second, these same medial regions showed selective, but negative, responses to the visual presentation of different stimulus categories, with clear preferences for scenes and faces.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through the six category functional localizer experiment.

claim: MPC regions were differentially recruited during memory recall of either people or places with a strong familiarity advantage.
source: Finally, and most critically, these regions were differentially recruited during memory recall of either people or places with a strong familiarity advantage.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through the memory recall experiment.

claim: The organizing principle defining the medial-lateral axis of VTC is reflected in MPC, but in the context of memory recall.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the organizing principle defining the medial-lateral axis of VTC is reflected in MPC, but in the context of memory recall.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by converging evidence from all three experiments.

claim: Human medial parietal cortex comprises a relatively large expanse of cortex, spanning the parieto-occipital sulcus to the splenium of the corpus collosum anteriorly and dorsally to include the precuneus and both the ventral and dorsal portions of the posterior cingulate cortex.
source: Human medial parietal cortex (MPC), a core component of the default mode network (DMN) (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010), comprises a relatively large expanse of cortex, spanning the parieto-occipital sulcus to the splenium of the corpus collosum anteriorly and dorsally to include the precuneus and both the ventral and dorsal portions of the posterior cingulate cortex (Bzdok et al., 2015).
evidence: This anatomical description is stated in the introduction with citation to Bzdok et al., 2015.

claim: MPC is associated with memory recall.
source: MPC is associated with a diverse set of cognitive functions, including (but not restricted to) memory recall (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008; Wagner et al., 2005; Gilmore et al., 2015; Kim, 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: MPC is associated with visual scene perception.
source: MPC is associated with a diverse set of cognitive functions, including (but not restricted to) memory recall (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008; Wagner et al., 2005; Gilmore et al., 2015; Kim, 2013) visual scene perception (Epstein et al., 2007; Silson et al., 2016; Baldassano et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MPC is associated with scene construction.
source: MPC is associated with a diverse set of cognitive functions, including (but not restricted to) memory recall (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008; Wagner et al., 2005; Gilmore et al., 2015; Kim, 2013) visual scene perception (Epstein et al., 2007; Silson et al., 2016; Baldassano et al., 2013), scene construction (Hassabis et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Hassabis et al., 2007.

claim: MPC is associated with processing of spatial and other contextual associations.
source: MPC is associated with a diverse set of cognitive functions, including (but not restricted to) memory recall (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008; Wagner et al., 2005; Gilmore et al., 2015; Kim, 2013) visual scene perception (Epstein et al., 2007; Silson et al., 2016; Baldassano et al., 2013), scene construction (Hassabis et al., 2007), processing of spatial and other contextual associations (Bar and Aminoff, 2003)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Bar and Aminoff, 2003.

claim: MPC is associated with navigation.
source: MPC is associated with a diverse set of cognitive functions, including (but not restricted to) memory recall (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008; Wagner et al., 2005; Gilmore et al., 2015; Kim, 2013) visual scene perception (Epstein et al., 2007; Silson et al., 2016; Baldassano et al., 2013), scene construction (Hassabis et al., 2007), processing of spatial and other contextual associations (Bar and Aminoff, 2003), navigation (Epstein, 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Epstein, 2008.

claim: MPC is associated with future thinking.
source: MPC is associated with a diverse set of cognitive functions, including (but not restricted to) memory recall (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008; Wagner et al., 2005; Gilmore et al., 2015; Kim, 2013) visual scene perception (Epstein et al., 2007; Silson et al., 2016; Baldassano et al., 2013), scene construction (Hassabis et al., 2007), processing of spatial and other contextual associations (Bar and Aminoff, 2003), navigation (Epstein, 2008), future thinking (Benoit and Schacter, 2015; Szpunar et al., 2007; Gilmore et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MPC is associated with mental orientation.
source: MPC is associated with a diverse set of cognitive functions, including (but not restricted to) memory recall (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008; Wagner et al., 2005; Gilmore et al., 2015; Kim, 2013) visual scene perception (Epstein et al., 2007; Silson et al., 2016; Baldassano et al., 2013), scene construction (Hassabis et al., 2007), processing of spatial and other contextual associations (Bar and Aminoff, 2003), navigation (Epstein, 2008), future thinking (Benoit and Schacter, 2015; Szpunar et al., 2007; Gilmore et al., 2016), and mental orientation (Peer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Peer et al., 2015.

claim: There is an absence of a clear consensus with regard to the function and overarching organization of MPC.
source: Given such diverse recruitment of MPC across cognitive domains historically considered largely independent (e.g. visual processing, memory), the absence of a clear consensus with regard to the function and overarching organization of MPC is perhaps unsurprising (Gilmore et al., 2015; Chrastil, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Network analyses using resting-state-functional-connectivity have identified either a single DMN 'hub' region or multiple networks.
source: Network analyses using resting-state-functional-connectivity (RSFC) have identified either a single DMN 'hub' region (Buckner et al. 2008) or multiple networks (Power et al., 2011; Braga and Buckner, 2017; Gilmore et al., 2018) that are often described as DMN subnetworks (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Yeo et al., 2011; Doucet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Task-based analyses suggest a fractionation of MPC beyond a single region.
source: Task-based analyses also suggest a fractionation beyond a single region (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Peer et al., 2015; Chrastil, 2018; Nelson et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The ventral and dorsal portions of posterior cingulate cortex interact differently with the rest of DMN during cognitive control.
source: Task-based analyses also suggest a fractionation beyond a single region (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Peer et al., 2015; Chrastil, 2018; Nelson et al., 2012) with, for example, evidence that the ventral and dorsal portions of posterior cingulate cortex interact differently with the rest of DMN during cognitive control (Leech et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Leech et al., 2011.

claim: Recent work has reframed MPC (and the DMN) in terms of large-scale cortical gradients.
source: Further, recent work has reframed MPC (and the DMN) in terms of large-scale cortical gradients (Margulies et al., 2016), conceptualizing MPC as the most abstract extension of the ventral visual pathway (Murphy et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MPC has been conceptualized as the most abstract extension of the ventral visual pathway.
source: Further, recent work has reframed MPC (and the DMN) in terms of large-scale cortical gradients (Margulies et al., 2016), conceptualizing MPC as the most abstract extension of the ventral visual pathway (Murphy et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Murphy et al., 2018 and Murphy et al., 2019.

claim: Divisions of MPC have been described along both the posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal axes in terms of cytoarchitecture.
source: Beyond MPC's link with the DMN, others have described divisions of MPC along both the posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal axes in terms of cytoarchitecture (Vogt, 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Vogt, 2009.

claim: Divisions of MPC have been described along both the posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal axes in terms of structural connectivity.
source: Beyond MPC's link with the DMN, others have described divisions of MPC along both the posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal axes in terms of cytoarchitecture (Vogt, 2009), structural connectivity (Parvizi et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Parvizi et al., 2006.

claim: Divisions of MPC have been described along both the posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal axes in terms of RSFC.
source: Beyond MPC's link with the DMN, others have described divisions of MPC along both the posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal axes in terms of cytoarchitecture (Vogt, 2009), structural connectivity (Parvizi et al., 2006), RSFC (Margulies et al., 2009; Vidaurre et al., 2018; Bzdok et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Divisions of MPC have been described along both the posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal axes in terms of electrocorticography.
source: Beyond MPC's link with the DMN, others have described divisions of MPC along both the posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal axes in terms of cytoarchitecture (Vogt, 2009), structural connectivity (Parvizi et al., 2006), RSFC (Margulies et al., 2009; Vidaurre et al., 2018; Bzdok et al., 2015), and electrocorticography (Foster and Parvizi, 2012; Daitch and Parvizi, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A small region of MPC directly anterior of scene-selective medial place area (MPA) showed strong functional connectivity with anterior portions of scene-selective parahippocampal place area (aPPA), located in medial VTC.
source: Specifically, a small region of MPC directly anterior of (visually) scene-selective medial place area (MPA) (Silson et al., 2016) showed strong functional connectivity with anterior portions of scene-selective parahippocampal place area (Epstein, 2008) (aPPA), located in medial VTC.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The connectivity-defined region between MPC and aPPA overlaps with regions of MPC engaged during memory recall.
source: This connectivity-defined region overlaps with regions of MPC engaged during memory recall (Silson et al., 2019), suggesting that the ventral/posterior aspect of MPC may contain distinct areas biased toward scene processing for vision and memory, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Silson et al., 2019.

claim: Multiple functional dimensions are thought to be represented along the medial-lateral axis of VTC, including category preference.
source: Indeed, multiple functional dimensions are thought to be represented along this axis, including category preference (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Deen et al., 2017) (e.g. scenes, objects, tools and faces)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Multiple functional dimensions are thought to be represented along the medial-lateral axis of VTC, including eccentricity.
source: Indeed, multiple functional dimensions are thought to be represented along this axis, including category preference (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Deen et al., 2017) (e.g. scenes, objects, tools and faces), eccentricity (Levy et al., 2001; Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017) (e.g. peripheral, foveal)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Multiple functional dimensions are thought to be represented along the medial-lateral axis of VTC, including animacy.
source: Indeed, multiple functional dimensions are thought to be represented along this axis, including category preference (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Deen et al., 2017) (e.g. scenes, objects, tools and faces), eccentricity (Levy et al., 2001; Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017) (e.g. peripheral, foveal), animacy (Konkle and Caramazza, 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Konkle and Caramazza, 2013.

claim: Multiple functional dimensions are thought to be represented along the medial-lateral axis of VTC, including real-world size.
source: Indeed, multiple functional dimensions are thought to be represented along this axis, including category preference (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Deen et al., 2017) (e.g. scenes, objects, tools and faces), eccentricity (Levy et al., 2001; Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017) (e.g. peripheral, foveal), animacy (Konkle and Caramazza, 2013), and even real-world size (Konkle and Oliva, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Konkle and Oliva, 2012.

claim: The mid-fusiform sulcus (MFS) has been identified as an anatomical landmark marking a transition point within each functional dimension in VTC.
source: Further, the mid-fusiform sulcus (MFS) (Weiner et al., 2014) has been identified as an anatomical landmark marking a transition point within each dimension (e.g. scene-selectivity medial of the MFS, face-selectivity lateral of the MFS).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Weiner et al., 2014.

claim: Scene-selectivity is medial of the MFS.
source: Further, the mid-fusiform sulcus (MFS) (Weiner et al., 2014) has been identified as an anatomical landmark marking a transition point within each dimension (e.g. scene-selectivity medial of the MFS, face-selectivity lateral of the MFS).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an example of the MFS as a transition point.

claim: Face-selectivity is lateral of the MFS.
source: Further, the mid-fusiform sulcus (MFS) (Weiner et al., 2014) has been identified as an anatomical landmark marking a transition point within each dimension (e.g. scene-selectivity medial of the MFS, face-selectivity lateral of the MFS).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an example of the MFS as a transition point.

claim: A ventral-posterior MPC region (MPCv) showed strongest connectivity with the anterior medial ROI of VTC.
source: A winner-take-all analysis (see Materials and methods) revealed a ventral-posterior MPC region (referred to as MPC ventral, MPCv) that showed strongest connectivity with the anterior medial ROI and an adjacent dorsal-anterior region (referred to as MPC dorsal, MPCd) that showed strongest connectivity to the anterior lateral ROI (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the resting-state functional connectivity experiment, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: A dorsal-anterior MPC region (MPCd) showed strongest connectivity to the anterior lateral ROI of VTC.
source: A winner-take-all analysis (see Materials and methods) revealed a ventral-posterior MPC region (referred to as MPC ventral, MPCv) that showed strongest connectivity with the anterior medial ROI and an adjacent dorsal-anterior region (referred to as MPC dorsal, MPCd) that showed strongest connectivity to the anterior lateral ROI (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the resting-state functional connectivity experiment, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Unlike category-selective regions of VTC, which typically exhibit positive responses to the presentation of visual stimuli, negative response magnitudes were observed to all categories within both MPC subdivisions.
source: Unlike category-selective regions of VTC (e.g. PPA, Fusiform Face Area, FFA), which typically exhibit positive responses to the presentation of visual stimuli, we observed negative response magnitudes to all categories within both MPC subdivisions.
evidence: This is a finding from the six category functional localizer experiment.

claim: Despite the general tendency for negative magnitudes, responses in MPC subdivisions differentiated on the basis of category, with scenes evoking the strongest response (i.e. least negative) in MPCv and faces evoking the strongest response in MPCd of both hemispheres.
source: Despite this general tendency for negative magnitudes, responses also appeared to differentiate on the basis of category, with scenes evoking the strongest response (i.e. least negative) in MPCv and faces evoking the strongest response in MPCd of both hemispheres (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the six category functional localizer experiment, shown in Figure 2.

claim: MPCv exhibited a significant main effect of Category in both the left (F(5, 140)=71.38, p<0.0001, partial η2 = 0.72) and right (F(5, 140)=49.46, p<0.0001, partial η2 = 0.64) hemispheres.
source: MPCv exhibited a significant main effect of Category in both the left (F(5, 140)=71.38, p<0.0001, partial η2 = 0.72) and right (F(5, 140)=49.46, p<0.0001, partial η2 = 0.64) hemispheres.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the six category functional localizer experiment.

claim: In MPCv, the response to scenes was significantly different from other stimulus categories in both hemispheres (t > 5.34, p<0.001, in all cases, Bonferroni corrected).
source: Consistent with the stronger functional connectivity with medial VTC, the response to scenes was significantly different from other stimulus categories in both hemispheres (t > 5.34, p<0.001, in all cases, Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the six category functional localizer experiment, shown in Figure 2a.

claim: MPCd exhibited a significant effect of Category within both left (F(5, 140)=19.28, p<0.0001, partial η2 = 0.48) and right F(5, 140)=12.66, p<0.0001, partial η2 = 0.31) hemispheres.
source: MPCd also exhibited a significant effect of Category within both left (F(5, 140)=19.28, p<0.0001, partial η2 = 0.48) and right F(5, 140)=12.66, p<0.0001, partial η2 = 0.31) hemispheres.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the six category functional localizer experiment.

claim: In MPCd left hemisphere, the response to faces was only significantly different from Buildings and Scrambled Objects (t > 3.86, p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected; p>0.05, in all other cases).
source: However, in this case the response to faces was only significantly different from Buildings and Scrambled Objects in the left hemisphere (t > 3.86, p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected; p>0.05, in all other cases)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the six category functional localizer experiment.

claim: In MPCd right hemisphere, the response to faces was significantly different from all categories except Objects (p>0.05) (t > 3.54, p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected).
source: whereas the response to faces was significantly different from all categories except Objects (p>0.05) in the right hemisphere (t > 3.54, p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the six category functional localizer experiment, shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The overall pattern of negative responses evoked by visual stimuli in MPC is consistent with the widely-reported negative responses within MPC (and the broader DMN) when orienting to external stimuli.
source: The overall pattern of negative responses evoked by visual stimuli is consistent with the widely-reported negative responses within MPC (and the broader DMN) when orienting to external stimuli27.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative responses with reference to prior literature (note: citation 27 appears to be a formatting error in the original).

claim: Within MPCv, responses were maximally positive (relative to baseline) for the recall of personally familiar places, whereas responses during recall of famous people were maximally negative.
source: Within MPCv, responses were maximally positive (relative to baseline) for the recall of personally familiar places, whereas responses during recall of famous people were maximally negative (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the memory recall experiment, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Within MPCd, responses were maximally positive for the recall of personally familiar people and maximally negative during recall of famous places.
source: In contrast, responses within MPCd were maximally positive for the recall of personally familiar people and maximally negative during recall of famous places (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the memory recall experiment, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Within MPCv, the main effects of Category (F(1, 23)=75.40 p=1.02−8, partial η2 = 0.76), Familiarity (F(1, 23)=128.61 p=6.78−11, partial η2 = 0.85) and Hemisphere (F(1, 23)=4.92 p=0.03, partial η2 = 0.17) were significant.
source: Within MPCv, the main effects of Category (F(1, 23)=75.40 p=1.02−8, partial η2 = 0.76), Familiarity (F(1, 23)=128.61 p=6.78−11, partial η2 = 0.85) and Hemisphere (F(1, 23)=4.92 p=0.03, partial η2 = 0.17) were significant, reflecting on average greater responses for the recall of places over people, personal over famous stimuli and in the right compared to left hemisphere, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the memory recall experiment.

claim: Within MPCv, there was a significant three-way interaction (Category by Familiarity by Hemisphere: F(1, 23)=7.19 p=0.01, partial η2 = 0.24).
source: However, these main effects were qualified by a significant three-way interaction (Category by Familiarity by Hemisphere: F(1, 23)=7.19 p=0.01, partial η2 = 0.24).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the memory recall experiment.

claim: The three-way interaction in MPCv reflects a larger familiarity difference (Personal >Famous) between categories (Place >People), in the right over left hemisphere.
source: This interaction reflects a larger familiarity difference (Personal >Famous) between categories (Place >People), in the right over left hemisphere.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical interaction from the memory recall experiment.

claim: In both hemispheres of MPCv, the Category by Familiarity interaction was significant (Left: F(1, 23)=31.19, p=0.00001, partial η2 = 0.56; Right: F(1, 23)=49.51, p=3.59−7, partial η2 = 0.68).
source: In both hemispheres, the Category by Familiarity interaction was significant (Left: F(1, 23)=31.19, p=0.00001, partial η2 = 0.56; Right: F(1, 23)=49.51, p=3.59−7, partial η2 = 0.68), reflecting a larger familiarity difference for the recall of places over people in both hemispheres (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the memory recall experiment, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Within MPCd, the main effects of Category (F(1, 23)=47.53 p=4.98−7, partial η2 = 0.67), Familiarity (F(1, 23)=82.33 p=4.62−9, partial η2 = 0.78) and Hemisphere (F(1, 23)=10.70 p=0.003, partial η2 = 0.32) were significant.
source: Within MPCd, the main effects of Category (F(1, 23)=47.53 p=4.98−7, partial η2 = 0.67), Familiarity (F(1, 23)=82.33 p=4.62−9, partial η2 = 0.78) and Hemisphere (F(1, 23)=10.70 p=0.003, partial η2 = 0.32) were again significant, reflecting on average greater responses for the recall of people over places, personal over famous stimuli and in the right compared to left hemisphere, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the memory recall experiment.

claim: Within MPCd, the Category by Familiarity interaction (F(1, 23)=7.89 p=0.01, partial η2 = 0.25) was significant.
source: Importantly, the Category by Familiarity interaction (F(1, 23)=7.89 p=0.01, partial η2 = 0.25), was significant, which reflects a larger familiarity difference for the recall of people over places with no clear difference between hemispheres (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the memory recall experiment, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Throughout MPC, the peak response during recall of personal people was always anterior and dorsal to the peak response during recall of personal places across all participants and hemispheres.
source: Across all participants and hemispheres, the peak response during recall of personal people was always anterior and dorsal to the peak response during recall of personal places (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the memory recall experiment, shown in Figure 5.

claim: At the whole-brain level, an alternating pattern of memory recall was observed along the ventral/posterior-dorsal/anterior axis of MPC: four adjacent subdivisions that alternated between being selectively recruited by the recall of places, then people, then places and finally people.
source: Most strikingly, along the ventral/posterior-dorsal/anterior axis of MPC, we observed an alternating pattern of memory recall: four adjacent subdivisions that alternated between being selectively recruited by the recall of places, then people, then places and finally people (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain Linear-Mixed-Effects analysis, shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The first two subdivisions identified in the whole-brain analysis (ROIs 1 and 2) were largely equivalent to the connectivity-defined MPCv and MPCd.
source: Notably, the first two subdivisions (refereed to here as ROIs 1 and 2) were largely equivalent to the connectivity-defined MPCv and MPCd (see Supplementary Material for spatial overlap).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary material.

claim: The whole-brain analysis revealed two anterior subdivisions within bilateral MPC (ROIs 3 and 4) that showed similar patterns of selective recruitment as the posterior subdivisions.
source: Thus, this analysis not only confirmed the differential recruitment during memory recall of MPCv and MPCd, but also, revealed two anterior subdivisions within bilateral MPC that showed similar patterns of selective recruitment (ROIs 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the whole-brain analysis findings.

claim: Strong memory recall for places was present in aPPA in both hemispheres.
source: Strong memory recall for places was also present in aPPA in both hemispheres (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis, shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The effect of familiarity manifested as an advantage for the recall of personally familiar over famous stimuli, irrespective of category within a relatively large swath of MPC.
source: In contrast to the alternating pattern of place and people recall, the effect of familiarity (collapsed across category) manifested as an advantage for the recall of personally familiar over famous stimuli, irrespective of category within a relatively large swath of MPC (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Between the odd and even splits of the memory data, the topography and magnitude of the effect of category was robust and highly correlated across splits and hemispheres (left hemisphere: r = 0.81, R2 = 0.65; right hemisphere: r = 0.84, R2 = 0.71).
source: Between the odd and even splits, the topography and magnitude of the effect of category was robust and highly correlated across splits and hemispheres, respectively (left hemisphere: r = 0.81, R2 = 0.65; right hemisphere: r = 0.84, R2 = 0.71) (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a finding from the split-half analysis, shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Recall of specific places selectively recruited ROIs 1 and 3 in the split-half analysis.
source: We observed a consistent and alternating pattern of selective recruitment throughout MPC. Recall of specific places selectively recruited ROIs 1 and 3, whereas recall of specific people selectively recruited ROIs 2 and 4.
evidence: This is a finding from the split-half analysis.

claim: Recall of specific people selectively recruited ROIs 2 and 4 in the split-half analysis.
source: We observed a consistent and alternating pattern of selective recruitment throughout MPC. Recall of specific places selectively recruited ROIs 1 and 3, whereas recall of specific people selectively recruited ROIs 2 and 4.
evidence: This is a finding from the split-half analysis.

claim: All four MPC subdivisions exhibited a familiarity advantage, which manifested as a selective enhancement in response for personally familiar items.
source: Consistent with our initial analyses, all four MPC subdivisions exhibited a familiarity advantage, which manifested as a selective enhancement in response for personally familiar items (Places = ROIs 1 and 3, People = ROIs, 2 and 4)
evidence: This is a finding from the split-half analysis.

claim: The posterior angular gyrus was recruited during place recall.
source: In particular, the posterior angular gyrus, inferior temporal sulcus, and superior frontal regions were recruited during place recall
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis of memory recall effects.

claim: The inferior temporal sulcus was recruited during place recall.
source: In particular, the posterior angular gyrus, inferior temporal sulcus, and superior frontal regions were recruited during place recall
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis of memory recall effects.

claim: Superior frontal regions were recruited during place recall.
source: In particular, the posterior angular gyrus, inferior temporal sulcus, and superior frontal regions were recruited during place recall
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis of memory recall effects.

claim: The recall of people recruited the insula and anterior temporal regions, particularly in the right hemisphere.
source: whereas the recall of people recruited the insula and anterior temporal regions, particularly in the right hemisphere (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Advantages for the recall of personally familiar stimuli were present within anterior cingulate cortex and insula in both hemispheres.
source: Advantages for the recall of personally familiar stimuli were present within anterior cingulate cortex and insula in both hemispheres (Figure 6b)
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Familiarity advantages were present in superior-frontal regions, superior-temporal sulcus, and angular gyrus/caudal inferior parietal lobule.
source: as well as regions on the lateral surface, including superior-frontal, the superior-temporal sulcus, and angular gyrus/caudal inferior parietal lobule (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recall effects associated with famous over familiar stimuli were sparse and non-significant.
source: In contrast, recall effects associated with famous over familiar stimuli were sparse and non-significant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing memory recall effects beyond MPC.

claim: Both PPA and FFA were recruited during recall of items from their preferred category.
source: Both regions were recruited during recall of items from their preferred category (i.e. greater response to place-specific memory in PPA, greater response to people-specific memory in FFA), although the magnitude of these memory effects were markedly weaker than within MPC (Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and see Supplementary file 1g for full statistical breakdown).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of VTC regions, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The magnitude of memory effects in PPA and FFA were markedly weaker than within MPC.
source: Both regions were recruited during recall of items from their preferred category (i.e. greater response to place-specific memory in PPA, greater response to people-specific memory in FFA), although the magnitude of these memory effects were markedly weaker than within MPC (Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and see Supplementary file 1g for full statistical breakdown).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of VTC regions, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hippocampus showed an effect of category, with larger responses during recall of places over people.
source: The hippocampus showed an effect of category, with larger responses during recall of places over people, whilst also showing a strong familiarity advantage with larger responses for personally familiar over famous stimuli (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of subcortical regions, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The hippocampus showed a strong familiarity advantage with larger responses for personally familiar over famous stimuli.
source: The hippocampus showed an effect of category, with larger responses during recall of places over people, whilst also showing a strong familiarity advantage with larger responses for personally familiar over famous stimuli (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of subcortical regions, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The amygdala showed only an effect of category, with larger responses during recall of people irrespective of the level of familiarity.
source: In contrast, the amygdala showed only an effect of category, with larger responses during recall of people irrespective of the level of familiarity (Figure 6—figure supplement 3; see Supplementary file 1h for full statistical breakdown).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of subcortical regions, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The selective recruitment of MPC during recall of places or people is consistent with a diverse literature linking MPC with multiple memory processes.
source: The selective recruitment of MPC during recall of places or people is consistent with a diverse literature linking MPC with multiple memory processes (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008; Wagner et al., 2005; Gilmore et al., 2015; Kim, 2013; McDermott et al., 1999; Gordon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The current study provides evidence for a set of functionally dissociable sub regions along the ventral/posterior-dorsal/anterior axis of MPC that appear selective for places and people, reminiscent of category-selective areas along the medial-lateral axis of VTC.
source: Unlike previous neuropsychological work (Valenstein et al., 1987; Arnott et al., 2008; Gainotti et al., 1998), which lacked the spatial specificity to examine the heterogeneity of MPC or neuroimaging work that has associated MPC divisions with broad domain-level processes (Wagner et al., 2005; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010), we provide evidence for a set of functionally dissociable sub regions along the ventral/posterior-dorsal/anterior axis of MPC that appear selective for places and people, reminiscent of category-selective areas along the medial-lateral axis of VTC.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key contribution of the work.

claim: During the recall of specific places, MPCv showed strong positive evoked responses, which contrasted with negative evoked responses during the recall of specific people.
source: During the recall of specific places, MPCv showed strong positive evoked responses, which contrasted with negative evoked responses during the recall of specific people.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing the memory recall findings.

claim: MPCd showed large positive evoked responses during recall of personally familiar people, but not during the recall of either famous people or places.
source: In contrast, MPCd showed largely the opposite pattern - large positive evoked responses during recall of personally familiar people, but not during the recall of either famous people or places.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing the memory recall findings.

claim: The division between ventral/posterior and dorsal/anterior portions of MPC based on the content of recalled memory is broadly consistent with prior anatomical and functional imaging work that also identified divisions within MPC along this axis.
source: This division is broadly consistent with prior anatomical (Vogt, 2009; Parvizi et al., 2006) and functional imaging (Margulies et al., 2009; Vidaurre et al., 2018; Foster and Parvizi, 2012; Margulies et al., 2016; Peer et al., 2015) work that also identified divisions within MPC along this axis, but did not do so on the basis of recalled content.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The cortical locations of MPCv/MPCd are consistent with previous observations of memory related activity.
source: The cortical locations of MPCv/MPCd are consistent with previous observations of memory related activity (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Peer et al., 2015; Gilmore et al., 2018; Kuhl and Chun, 2014; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The locations of MPCv/MPCd are qualitatively similar to regions recruited when participants mentally oriented by making egocentric distance judgments between two places or between two people.
source: Indeed, the locations of MPCv/MPCd are qualitatively similar to regions recruited when participant's mentally oriented by either making egocentric distance judgments between two places (i.e. which location is physically closest to them), or between two people (i.e. which of two people are personally closer to them), respectively (Peer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Peer et al., 2015.

claim: An explicit distance task is not required to functionally isolate MPCv and MPCd.
source: Although such a distance judgement undoubtedly requires recalling specific information, our findings suggest that an explicit distance task is not required to functionally isolate MPCv and MPCd.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the current findings.

claim: The anterior pair of MPC regions falls anterior of the 'place' and 'people' regions reported by Peer et al. (2015).
source: Importantly, we also identify a second pair of anterior regions along the same ventral/posterior-dorsal/anterior axis, that fall anterior of the 'place' and 'people' regions reported by Peer et al. (2015), revealing a total of four subdivisions selectively recruited during memory recall for people or places in an alternating pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion comparing the current findings to Peer et al., 2015.

claim: The pattern of selective recruitment in the anterior pair of MPC regions remained despite an overall reduction in the magnitude of responses to recalled stimuli, as compared to MPCv/MPCd.
source: One intriguing feature of this anterior pair of regions was that the pattern of selective recruitment remained despite an overall reduction in the magnitude of responses to recalled stimuli, as compared to MPCv/MPCd.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion describing the anterior pair of regions.

claim: The location of the anterior pair of MPC regions appears qualitatively similar to the 'time' region identified by Peer et al. (2015).
source: The location of this anterior pair appears qualitatively similar to the 'time' region identified by Peer et al. (2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Peer et al., 2015.

claim: A recent meta-analysis found that a ventral/posterior region of MPC was more likely to be recruited during scene and navigation-related tasks, whilst more dorsal/anterior portions were more likely to be involved in theory-of-mind and social/emotional tasks.
source: For example, a recent meta-analysis attempted to divide a ventral portion of MPC (referred to as retrosplenial complex) on the basis of different fMRI task activations (Chrastil, 2018). Although the majority of MPC was found to be recruited during memory tasks, a ventral/posterior region was more likely to be recruited during scene and navigation-related tasks, whilst more dorsal/anterior portions were more likely to be involved in theory-of-mind and social/emotional tasks.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Chrastil, 2018.

claim: A recent report separated social regions of MPC (i.e. those engaged with theory-of-mind tasks) from those involved with constructive memory or the formation of contextual associations.
source: Similarly, a recent report (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010) separated social regions of MPC (i.e. those engaged with theory-of-mind tasks) from those involved with constructive memory or the formation of contextual associations (Hassabis et al., 2007; Bar and Aminoff, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The dorsal and ventral divisions of MPC align well with recent studies that have attempted to map social network representations and representations of familiar scenes, respectively.
source: The dorsal and ventral divisions also align well with recent studies that have attempted to map social network representations (Parkinson et al., 2017) and representations of familiar scenes (Sugiura et al., 2005), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The robust memory recall effects in MPC were evoked by the relatively simple task of recalling items that were cued by word stimuli only.
source: Perhaps more importantly, these robust effects were evoked by the relatively simple task of recalling items that were cued by word stimuli only (or even merely perceiving presented stimuli), as opposed to performing more complex contextual association (Hassabis et al., 2007), navigation (Chrastil, 2018), social judgment (Parkinson et al., 2017), or mental orientation tasks (Peer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion highlighting the simplicity of the paradigm.

claim: Strong recruitment of MPC through a simple paradigm is consistent with recent work showing that MPC (and the larger DMN) plays a role in simple spatial judgments of shapes and objects, particularly when made from memory.
source: Such strong recruitment of MPC through a simple paradigm is consistent with recent work showing that MPC (and the larger DMN) plays a role in simple spatial judgments of shapes and objects, particularly when made from memory (Konishi et al., 2015; Murphy et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The DMN has more recently been divided into two or three subnetworks.
source: Although initially conceived as a singular entity (Raichle et al., 2001), the DMN has more recently been divided into two (Shirer et al., 2012) or three (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010) subnetworks.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In the 'three network' framework, much of MPC and ventral medial prefrontal cortex act as a 'core' that flexibly integrates information between the 'dorsal' and 'ventral' subnetworks.
source: In the 'three network' framework, much of MPC and ventral medial prefrontal cortex act as a 'core' that flexibly integrates information between the 'dorsal' and 'ventral' subnetworks (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010.

claim: The current results challenge the 'core' conceptualization of MPC by suggesting that MPC is fractionated along the same lines as the DMN subnetworks.
source: Our results challenge this 'core' conceptualization by suggesting that MPC is fractionated along the same lines as these subnetworks
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The dorsal component of the DMN, which overlapped regions recruited during people memory, is associated with social/semantic processing.
source: the dorsal component of the DMN, which overlapped regions recruited during people memory, is associated with social/semantic processing (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010) (Figure 8a)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The ventral component of the DMN, which is often referred to as a 'scene construction' or 'contextual association' network, overlaps with regions recruited during place memory.
source: while, the ventral component, which is often referred to as a 'scene construction' or 'contextual association' (Hassabis et al., 2007; Bar and Aminoff, 2003) network overlaps with regions recruited during place memory (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations and shown in Figure 8b.

claim: In the 'two network' framework, the DMN is comprised of dorsal and ventral subnetworks without a clear integrative 'core'.
source: In the 'two network' framework (Shirer et al., 2012) the DMN is comprised of dorsal and ventral subnetworks without a clear integrative 'core'.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Shirer et al., 2012.

claim: Recent work using highly-sampled participants identified two parallel and interdigitated networks spanning cortex that both appeared to overlap with the canonical DMN.
source: This framework is also consistent with recent work using highly-sampled participants to identify two parallel and interdigitated networks spanning cortex (Braga and Buckner, 2017). These two functional networks—both of which appeared to overlap with the canonical DMN—could be differentiated through functional connectivity, given sufficient data, but stopped short of describing their specific functional organization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Braga and Buckner, 2017.

claim: The current data provide a possible functional account of the two interdigitated networks by anchoring them to differential recruitment based on the content of perceived images as well as recalled memories.
source: Our data provide a possible functional account of these networks by anchoring them to differential recruitment based on the content of perceived images as well as recalled memories, and moreover, demonstrate that such an interdigitated pattern of regions can be identified at the group-level given appropriate tasks.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The MPC regions reported appear to overlap with the recently proposed 'posterior medial' (PM) memory system.
source: The MPC regions we report also appear to overlap with the recently proposed 'posterior medial' (PM) memory system and the effects we observe are broadly consistent with the notion that the PM system is involved in recollecting episodic details, constructive uses of memory, and social cognition (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012.

claim: The present work suggests a differentiation within the PM system based on the recall of places and people, which was not discussed originally.
source: However, the present work suggests a differentiation within the PM system based on the recall of places and people, which was not discussed originally, suggesting that MPC's role in memory recall does not fit neatly into a simple 'binary systems' model.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A parietal memory network (PMN) has been identified, which includes regions within both lateral parietal cortex and MPC that are thought to be distinct from those within the DMN/PM system.
source: More recently, a parietal memory network (PMN) (Gilmore et al., 2015; McDermott et al., 2017) has been identified, which includes regions within both lateral parietal cortex and MPC that are thought to be distinct from those within the DMN/PM (Yang et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2019; Gilmore et al., 2019a; Gilmore et al., 2019b) system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The memory effects reported overlap with DMN regions and appear close to, but separate from, those within the PMN.
source: The memory effects we report overlap with DMN regions and appear close to, but separate from, those within the PMN (i.e., do not extend to mid-cingulate cortex or posterior aspects of the precuneus).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion describing the relationship to the PMN.

claim: Category-selectivity is one organizing principle thought to define the medial-lateral axis of VTC.
source: Category-selectivity is one organizing principle thought to define the medial-lateral axis of VTC.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Even at early stages of cortical development, category-selective regions appear in stereotypical locations across individuals.
source: Even at early stages of cortical development (Deen et al., 2017; Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017), category-selective regions appear in stereotypical locations across individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The pattern of functional-connectivity, perceptual and memory recall effects reported are consistent with the presence of categorical organization within MPC.
source: The pattern of functional-connectivity, perceptual and memory recall effects we report are consistent with the presence of this motif within MPC.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Eccentricity varies systematically along the medial-lateral axis of VTC.
source: For example, eccentricity also varies systematically along the medial-lateral axis of VTC (Levy et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Levy et al., 2001.

claim: Eccentricity representations in VTC are highly correlated with category preference (e.g. PPA is peripherally biased, whereas FFA is foveally biased).
source: Indeed, these eccentricity representations are so highly correlated with category preference (e.g. PPA is peripherally biased, whereas FFA is foveally biased) that eccentricity has been suggested to form a prototypical organization onto which such selectivity later develops with visual experience (Silson et al., 2015; Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: It is possible that the development of categorical-preference in VTC during perception drives the development of categorical-preference in MPC for memory.
source: It may be that the selective recruitment we observe in MPC during memory recall arises in a similar manner: That is, it is possible that the development of categorical-preference in VTC during perception drives the development of categorical-preference in MPC for memory.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation about the developmental relationship.

claim: The conceptualization of the DMN as an abstract extension of VTC is compatible with the proposition that categorical preference in VTC drives categorical preference in MPC.
source: Such a proposition is compatible with recent work focusing on large-scale cortical gradients that conceptualized the DMN, including MPC, as an abstract extension of VTC (Margulies et al., 2016), although in the current study we observed effects that appeared to follow a distinct regional—rather than gradient-like—organization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Margulies et al., 2016.

claim: It is possible that the manner in which mnemonic representations of places and people are encoded and retrieved in MPC differ in a way reminiscent of how the visual perception of places and people in VTC differ in terms of peripheral/foveal stimulation.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that the manner in which mnemonic representations of places and people are encoded and retrieved in MPC, differ in a way reminiscent of how the visual perception of places and people in VTC differ in terms of peripheral/foveal stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an alternative speculation, with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The organization of category representations in the brain are determined by the underlying structural (i.e. anatomical) and functional (e.g. perceptual) template.
source: Importantly, these accounts are consistent with theories that suggest the organization of category representations in the brain are determined by the underlying structural (i.e. anatomical) and functional (e.g. perceptual) template (Martin, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Martin, 2016.

claim: Responses in VTC during perception are characterized by larger evoked positive responses to stimuli of the preferred category.
source: For instance, responses in VTC during perception are characterized by larger evoked positive responses to stimuli of the preferred category (Silson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Silson et al., 2016.

claim: Perceptual responses within MPCv/MPCd were best characterized by negative evoked responses that were attenuated, although not extinguished, by category-preference.
source: In contrast, perceptual responses within MPCv/MPCd were best characterized by negative evoked responses that were attenuated, although not extinguished, by category-preference.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing the perceptual findings.

claim: There was no clear relationship between the positively and negatively evoked responses between the VTC regions and their paired MPC region at the across participant level.
source: Despite appearing to share category representations, there was no clear relationship between the positively and negatively evoked responses between the VTC regions and their paired MPC region (e.g. anterior medial VTC – MPCv), at least at the across participant level.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion describing the relationship between VTC and MPC responses.

claim: The negative BOLD response in MPC is consistent with the widely-observed 'task-negative' activation of the larger DMN and the MPC component of it.
source: Although the relationship between negative BOLD-signal changes and the underlying neural activity is an area of ongoing research (Shmuel et al., 2002; Shmuel et al., 2006) and has been associated with inhibition in visual cortex (Smith et al., 2004), this response is consistent with the widely-observed 'task-negative' activation of the larger DMN and the MPC component of it (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Sixty-five participants completed the resting-state functional connectivity experiment.
source: Resting-state functional connectivity experiment: Sixty-five participants (40 female), mean age = 24.67 ± 3.2 years) completed the resting-state functional connectivity experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Twenty-nine participants completed the functional localizer experiment.
source: Six category functional Localizer experiment: Twenty-nine participants (21 female, mean age = 24.2 years) completed the functional localizer experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Twenty-four participants completed the memory experiment.
source: Memory experiment: Twenty-four participants (17 female, mean age = 24.2 years) completed the memory experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The sample size for the memory experiment was based on prior work from the research group employing a very similar paradigm.
source: The sample size for the memory experiment was based on prior work from our group (Silson et al., 2019) employing a very similar paradigm.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citation to Silson et al., 2019.
